title: On Consensus and Humming in the IETF
summary: Explains how the IETF's rough consensus process is meant to work and why it is not majority voting. It argues the IETF has drifted toward vote-like behavior and suggests ways to get back to real rough consensus. It is informational and does not change process.

eli5.summary: Instead of raising hands to count votes, a group hums to feel the mood, and makes sure everyone's worries are heard first.

questions: how does the ietf make decisions
subtitle: Why the IETF decides by open issues rather than by votes, and what humming is really for.

tldr.problem: Some IETF participants and chairs treat hums and polls as votes, then ask why the discussion is not over once a hum has happened. Working groups end up factious, with long-running unresolved issues and bad compromises.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains that rough consensus means every objection has been addressed, though not necessarily accommodated. Counting heads does not decide it, and a hum is only a way to start the conversation.
tldr.outcome: It is a call for thought and discussion rather than a new procedure. It prescribes no specific process, and says current practice does not always match its principles.

today: RFC 7282 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes principles rather than a fixed procedure, and says it is meant to generate thought and discussion.

sections.title: Rough Consensus and Running Code
sections.content:
The IETF's credo, from Dave Clark's 1992 plenary talk, is "We reject: kings, presidents and voting. We believe in: rough consensus and running code." Decisions come from the consent of participants, allowing some dissent, rather than from one individual or a vote.

Full consensus would be ideal but is not required, since one person saying "No!" could halt everything. If a working group chair finds that a technical issue raised by an objector has been truly considered and the group has made an informed decision that the objection is answered or is not enough to block progress, the chair can declare rough consensus. Chairs sometimes ask for a hum instead of a show of hands to underline that nobody is voting.

The RFC says it has seen misunderstandings: people asking "Why don't we just vote?" or "We've already hummed, so why isn't the discussion concluded?". It aims to foster understanding, not to dictate procedure, and admits that many current practices are not consistent with its principles.
sections.eli5: Nobody gets to be the boss and nobody just counts hands. The group works until the worries have all been answered.

sections.title: Objections Matter More Than Agreement
sections.content:
The RFC's example: a chair asks "Is everyone OK with format A?", gets objections, then asks about format B and gets more. The chair is stuck because they sought agreement. But determining consensus and coming to consensus differ from having it. The key is to separate choices that are merely unappealing from those that are truly problematic.

A better question is "Can anyone not live with choice A?", followed by asking why. Objectors may convince the group, or be convinced that the concern is only a matter of taste. Silence and apathy are not consensus either: it needs the active engagement of those doing the work.

The RFC separates two kinds of compromise. Compromising between engineering tradeoffs is expected. Compromising between people is harmful when it is capitulation ("Forget it, do what you want") or horse-trading ("I'll stop objecting to yours if you stop objecting to mine"), because the real objections stay unaddressed.
sections.eli5: Asking "who agrees?" gets arguments. Asking "what is the one thing you cannot live with?" finds the real problems quickly.

sections.title: Addressed Is Not the Same as Accommodated
sections.content:
Rough consensus is reached when every issue has been addressed, but not necessarily accommodated. A working group may agree that an objection is a real shortcoming and still judge that fixing it is not worth the tradeoff, for example choosing a well-understood protocol over a more elegant untested one. The chair can then declare rough consensus despite continued objection.

This relies on the chair's judgement. The group must truly weigh the issue, and the chair needs a good idea of the work's purpose and architecture, perhaps from the charter or a requirements document. The chair cannot base a decision only on many voices saying "the objection isn't valid", which would just be a vote. The objector should get a reasoned explanation, and can appeal. A technical error is always a valid basis for appeal.

The RFC contrasts this with RFC 1603, which described rough consensus as the "dominant view", and with RFC 2418, which said 51% does not qualify and 99% is better than rough. This document disagrees that balloting or percentages can determine consensus.
sections.eli5: The group can say "we heard you, you are right that it is a problem, but we still choose this way, and here is why." That is allowed, but they have to really explain.

sections.title: What Humming Is For
sections.content:
The IETF does not vote partly because it has no members, only participants, so it is nearly impossible to say who would get a vote. Final decisions are supposed to be made on the mailing list, by looking at open issues. A hum is not an anonymous vote, and judging by the loudest hum is almost certainly a mis-assessment.

Good reasons to hum: to find a starting point when the room seems split, since the chair can begin with the objections to the option with more support, and to take the temperature of the room. A hum can show that a smaller group feels strongly against a more popular choice. The RFC also warns that hums have pitfalls. Some people hum louder than others, the wording and order of the question affect the result, and a poll at the end can discourage a minority from speaking up.

If a chair already senses consensus, a better move is to say so and ask whether anyone has concerns. Even a coin flip can pick where to start, as has happened in working groups, but the flip does not decide the outcome. The hum begins the discussion; it does not end it.
sections.eli5: A hum is like peeking to see which way the class is leaning, so the teacher knows where to start talking. It does not decide anything.

sections.title: Numbers Versus Open Issues
sections.content:
The RFC argues that open issues, not head counts, decide whether consensus exists. In its first example, over 100 people support a protocol, but a few point out that it has no way to back off under congestion, and the objection gets only silence. Even if 100 people reply to a last call that the document is ready, the unaddressed issue means there is no consensus, not even rough consensus.

The reverse case is deliberately controversial. Five expert participants agree on a protocol, one objector's preferred algorithm is considered and set aside as riskier than the well-understood one, and the objector then recruits one hundred people to post support for it. When the chair asks them for new technical information and gets silence, the chair may still find rough consensus. The RFC calls this a degenerate case that signals something pathological, and notes that it would be very hard for an appeals body to sort out. Its point is that rough consensus guards against vote stuffing.

Consensus is a tool, not a goal: voting leads to gaming, wrong-sort compromises, ignored minorities and worse technical outcomes.
sections.eli5: If one kid points out the bridge has a hole, a hundred kids shouting "build it" do not fix the hole. The hole still has to be dealt with.

sections.title: Conclusion and Security Note
sections.content:
The conclusion says the document is not really about procedures. It describes a way of thinking about how the IETF makes decisions, so that participants avoid the dangers of majority rule and reach rough consensus decisions with the best technical outcomes. A show of hands can be useful or damaging, and a hum can be a good device or a poorly disguised vote.

The Security Considerations section contains only a quotation from Lao Tzu: "He who defends with love will be secure."
sections.eli5: The big idea is to think about why you decide things a certain way, so you end up with the best answer and not just the loudest one.
